investment_summary:
Amazon's FY2025 10-K shows faster growth and higher profit, but weaker cash generation. Net sales rose 12% to $716.9 billion, AWS grew 20%, and operating income rose to $80.0 billion from $68.6 billion [1]. Normalized income rose 7% to $65.4 billion, but free cash flow fell to $11.2 billion from $38.2 billion as cash capex reached $128.3 billion [1].

The valuation asks for more than consensus. The reverse DCF at the current enterprise value implies 19.2% annual revenue growth for ten years, above FY2026 consensus growth of 15.7% and the 11.7% three-year historical CAGR [2][3]. Consensus and post-filing figures are dated after the 10-K. The implied return of 8.3% sits below a 12.4% WACC [3]. The current price therefore needs AWS growth to hold and capex to convert into cash. Liquidity was adequate at year-end, with $123.0 billion of cash and securities [1], but total debt has risen since then [2]. Main risks are fixed-cost capacity planning, competition, and legal and tax outcomes [1].
key_takeaways: AWS growth should keep funding the capex cycle, though its profit is lagging sales: AWS sales rose 20% while operating income rose only 14% [1].
Capex should start converting to cash, but free cash flow fell to $11.2 billion from $38.2 billion as spending reached $128.3 billion [1].
Valuation looks demanding: the current enterprise value implies 19.2% revenue growth, above 15.7% FY2026 consensus [2][3].
Funding is the watch item: total debt rose to $271.9 billion by September 2026 while trailing free cash flow turned negative [2].
business_overview:
Amazon.com, Inc., founded in 1994, is a multi-segment retailer and technology company. It reports three segments: North America, International, and Amazon Web Services (AWS). Products are sold through online and physical stores, a third-party seller marketplace, and a fulfillment network, and cloud computing is provided through AWS [1]. Management states that low prices and fast delivery are central to its strategy. At December 31, 2025, the company employed about 1,576,000 people [1].

Its core offer combines scale with subscriptions. Prime includes fast, free shipping on tens of millions of items plus video, live sports, and other benefits. The company also manufactures devices including Kindle, Fire, Echo, Ring, and eero, and runs seller and advertising programs [1]. AWS offers compute, storage, database, analytics, and artificial intelligence services. The filing places the company across e-commerce, cloud infrastructure, digital media, and advertising, with competitors ranging from retailers and cloud providers to search engines and healthcare providers [1].

2025 combined heavy investment with some one-off items. Cash capital expenditures rose to $128.3 billion from $77.7 billion, mostly for technology infrastructure supporting AWS [1]. The company recorded a $2.5 billion FTC settlement charge and $2.7 billion of severance tied to planned role eliminations [1]. It invested $2.7 billion in Anthropic convertible notes, and a price adjustment on that stake drove most of the $15.2 billion of other income [1]. Planned 2026 initiatives include satellite broadband, autonomous ride-hailing vehicles, quick commerce, and sharper international prices [1].

The segment mix shows where the economics sit. North America generated 59% of 2025 net sales ($426.3 billion), International 23% ($161.9 billion), and AWS 18% ($128.7 billion) [1]. AWS contributed $45.6 billion of the $80.0 billion total segment operating income, about 57%, although it is under a fifth of sales [1].
market_position:
Amazon's end markets are global but weighted toward the United States. North America generated 59% of 2025 net sales, International 23%, and AWS 18% [1]. The filing does not disclose market share for any segment, so the company's position has to be inferred from scale and growth rather than a reported share figure [1]. Against the peers in this report, Amazon has the largest revenue base in the shared years, while its growth sits at the lower end of the group [4].

Customer concentration is not disclosed, so the filing cannot confirm whether major customers are blue-chip companies [1]. What is visible is a broad base: hundreds of millions of products sold by Amazon and third parties, Prime members, advertisers, and AWS customers [1]. Management says AI-enabled tools lower barriers for smaller competitors, which the filing flags as a source of pressure [1]. Within AWS, pricing is partly set by long-term customer contracts, which the filing cites as offsetting usage growth [1].

The market's view of the stock is on the record. Consensus FY2026 revenue is $829.2 billion, implying 15.7% growth, with a forward EV/Sales of 3.6x at the current enterprise value [3]. Consensus rating is Buy, with a mean target price of $326.34 (range $230 to $405) [3]. These consensus figures are dated after the 10-K. Amazon is best classified as a scale leader in its core e-commerce and cloud markets, but the filing gives no share data to confirm that position [1].
operating_results:
Net sales rose 12% to $716.9 billion from $638.0 billion in 2025 [1]. AWS (+20%) and International (+13%) grew faster than North America (+10%) [1]. Cost of sales grew 9%, slower than sales, and fell to 49.7% of sales from 51.1%, lifting gross margin to 50.3% from 48.9% [1]. Technology and infrastructure spending rose 23% and is the main cost pressure [1]. Operating income rose to $80.0 billion from $68.6 billion, despite $5.2 billion of FTC settlement and severance charges [1].

Reported earnings are distorted below operating income. Net income includes a net gain of about $15 billion in other income, tied mainly to the Anthropic investment, so diluted EPS rose to $7.17 from $5.53 [1]. Normalized income, which excludes that gain, rose 7% to $65.4 billion, and that is the better measure of operating earnings growth [1]. Cash taxes fell to $8.3 billion from $12.3 billion under the 2025 Tax Act, which flattered operating cash flow [1]. Operating cash flow rose to $139.5 billion from $115.9 billion, but free cash flow fell to $11.2 billion from $38.2 billion [1].

Segment results show where the margin came from. North America operating income rose 19% to $29.6 billion, lifting its margin to about 7.0% [1]. International operating income rose 25% to $4.8 billion, but foreign exchange contributed $903 million, and excluding it the gain was about 1.5% [1]. AWS operating income rose 14% to $45.6 billion, slower than AWS sales growth of 20%, as infrastructure spending absorbed much of the sales gain [1]. First-quarter 2026 operating income guidance of $16.5 to $21.5 billion compares with $18.4 billion a year earlier [1].
risk_assessment:
The first risk is intense competition that can force lower prices or higher spending. The filing names more than a dozen segments where Amazon competes, including retail, cloud, advertising, grocery, healthcare, and logistics [1]. Some competitors have greater resources, longer histories, and more brand recognition, and may secure better vendor terms and adopt more aggressive pricing [1]. The company says competition could require it to increase spending or lower prices, which could materially reduce sales and profits [1]. The filing gives no market share or margin data for this risk, so it cannot be sized from the filing alone.

The second risk is a large fixed-cost base and forecasting error. The filing says a significant portion of expenses and investments is fixed, and the company may not adjust spending quickly enough if sales fall short [1]. Forecast errors can leave excess or insufficient fulfillment and data-center capacity, with impairment charges and inventory write-downs [1]. Demand can fluctuate with recessionary fears or inflation, and a disproportionate share of retail sales falls in the fourth quarter [1]. The stakes are rising with capex: $128.3 billion of cash capex in 2025 adds to fixed commitments [1].

The third risk is legal, regulatory, and tax proceedings. The filing discloses competition and consumer-protection investigations affecting stores, fulfillment, Prime, and parts of AWS, along with litigation brought by state attorneys general and the FTC [1]. An Indian tax authority assertion covers cloud services fees, and the filing says audit outcomes could differ materially from historical accruals [1]. The company says outcomes are inherently unpredictable and losses above recorded amounts are possible [1]. The $2.5 billion FTC settlement charge in 2025 shows the cost can be large [1].

The balance sheet adds a funding dimension. Long-term debt rose to $65.6 billion from $52.6 billion [1]. Yahoo shows total debt of $153.0 billion at FY2025 and $271.9 billion at September 30, 2026, with trailing free cash flow of -$37.6 billion [2]. Those later figures are dated after the 10-K. Liquidity was adequate at year-end, with $123.0 billion of cash and securities against current liabilities that were close to current assets [1]. The Piotroski F-Score of 6 of 9 and Altman Z-Score of 5.74 show no distress signal [2], though the Z-Score is designed for manufacturers and may be less reliable here.
competitors_analysis:
Against Microsoft, Alphabet, and Walmart, Amazon's profitability and returns improved sharply between 2022 and 2025, but its cash conversion weakened [4]. Amazon was chosen alongside these peers for business model first: Microsoft competes with AWS in cloud, Alphabet competes in advertising, and Walmart is the closest retail peer by revenue scale in the candidate list. Coupang and eBay were excluded as far smaller than Amazon.

Amazon's gross margin rose each year, from 43.8% in 2022 to 50.3% in 2025, but it remained well below Microsoft (68.8%) and Alphabet (59.7%) in 2025 and well above Walmart's 24–25% range [4]. Its EBITDA margin rose from 7.5% to 23.1% over the same period, still below Alphabet's 44.9% and Microsoft's 55.2% in 2025 [4]. Revenue growth of 12.4% in 2025 was below Microsoft's 14.9% growth in the same year and below Alphabet's 15.1%, though above Walmart's 5.1% [4].

Return on invested capital is the clearest weakness. Amazon's ROIC was 16.8% in 2025, down from 18.1% in 2024, and trailed Microsoft (26.8%) and Alphabet (28.7%), with Walmart at 17.1% [4]. Free cash flow conversion of 0.10 was the lowest of the four in 2025, below Walmart's 0.65, Alphabet's 0.55, and Microsoft's 0.70 [4]. The stated conversion values do not reconcile to a simple FCF over EBITDA calculation, so they should be treated with caution.

Valuation is where the picture reverses. Amazon's EV/EBITDA fell to 15.4 in 2025, the lowest of the four, against Microsoft at 24.0, Alphabet at 21.1, and Walmart at 20.0 [4]. Read against the 10-K, the lower multiple reflects the market discounting weak cash conversion rather than a clear mispricing [1][4]. The consensus Buy rating and $326.34 mean target price are dated after the 10-K and do not change this peer read [3]. Revenue and margin trends support the business, while the cash line is the variable that decides whether the discount is deserved [1][4].

investment_theses.thesis: AWS keeps growing fast enough to justify its spending.
investment_theses.evidence: AWS sales rose 20% to $128.7 billion in 2025, but operating income rose only 14% to $45.6 billion [1].
investment_theses.signpost: AWS operating income grows in line with or faster than AWS sales in each 2026 quarterly report.
investment_theses.invalidation: AWS sales growth below 15%, or AWS operating income falling year over year in any 2026 quarter.

investment_theses.thesis: Capex starts converting to free cash flow in 2026.
investment_theses.evidence: 2025 free cash flow was $11.2 billion versus $38.2 billion in 2024 [1]. Yahoo trailing free cash flow at 2026-09-30 was -$37.6 billion [2].
investment_theses.signpost: Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow is positive at the FY2026 10-K, filed early 2027.
investment_theses.invalidation: Trailing free cash flow is still negative at FY2026 year-end.

investment_theses.thesis: The valuation needs growth above consensus, so any slowdown hits the stock.
investment_theses.evidence: The reverse DCF implies 19.2% growth versus 15.7% FY2026 consensus; implied IRR is 8.3% versus a 12.4% WACC [2][3]. Current-year EPS consensus fell from $12.93 to $12.80 over 30 days [3].
investment_theses.signpost: FY2026 revenue consensus stays at or above 15.7% in the Q4 2026 update.
investment_theses.invalidation: Consensus growth falls below 14%, or EPS revisions stay negative for two more quarters.

investment_theses.thesis: Debt growth outpaces cash generation, adding funding risk.
investment_theses.evidence: Total debt rose from $153.0 billion at FY2025 to $271.9 billion at 2026-09-30, and net cash fell to -$157.7 billion [2].
investment_theses.signpost: Total debt stops rising at the FY2026 10-K.
investment_theses.invalidation: Debt keeps rising while trailing free cash flow stays negative.
